newsitem.title: FRANCE: Israeli minister says Syria peace talks not frozen.
newsitem.headline: Israeli minister says Syria peace talks not frozen.

text.p: Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said after meeting French President Jacques Chirac on Friday that peace talks with Syria were not frozen and that France wanted to help narrow Israeli-Syrian differences.

Levy's visit to Paris marked a warming of relations between the two countries after Chirac's confrontation with Israeli security men in Jerusalem in October dramatised differences over the terms for peace, the role of Europe and the city's status.

Referring to a meeting in Damascus on Wednesday between European envoy Miguel Angel Moratinos and Syrian President Hafez al-Assad, Levy told reporters: "I have been informed that Syria was interested in the statements I made recently on the need to restart negotiations and on the formula which would allow this."
He added: "In any case this affair is not frozen."
Peace talks with Syria were suspended by Israel's previous government after a wave of Islamist attacks 11 months ago, but Levy would not be drawn on a date for a relaunch.
"You think I can impose a date on the Syrians?" he asked.

Asked whether he had asked Chirac to pass a message on to the Syrians, Levy answered: "I did not ask him (to do that). The French want to reduce the gap between Israelis and Syrians. They know that there is now a chance to do that."
Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna quoted him as stressing that Levy was the first senior figure from the region he had met since the signing of the Hebron accords earlier this month.
"Chirac said after the meeting that he was happy to note the Israeli government's determination to go forward and continue the peace process," Colonna said.

"The atmosphere was friendly. We are going to continue to develop our relations which are good despite some differences. Several French ministers are going to visit us soon," Levy said. French Defence Minister Charles Millon would visit Israel in February.

On his Middle East tour, Chirac pleaded for a Palestinian state and the return of occupied Arab land to Syria and Lebanon. He also berated heavy-handed Israeli security men who "protected" him from contact with Palestinians in Jerusalem's Old City.

Levy said he had insisted on the need to maintain peace in southern Lebanon. The deaths of three Israeli soldiers in an explosion on Thursday was unacceptable and Syria bore a "direct responsibility" in the deaths, he said.
Iranian-backed Hizbollah guerrillas claimed responsibility for the attack in which three soldiers were killed and one wounded by a roadside bomb.

Syria demands Israel resume the talks from the point at which they stopped, insisting the previous Israeli government had approved the principle of full withdrawal from the Golan Heights, seized by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu opposes the land-for-peace formula which has been the basis for five years of negotiations. Israel's previous government said it was willing to make at least a partial return of the Golan.
